text: Version control for notebooks and pipelines — what actually gets committed, and why it has to be readable.
A notebook's committed source is its code, not its output. Output changes every run even when the code doesn't — committing it alongside the code would generate a meaningless diff every single time.
A KQL queryset's definition is a readable JSON file, so a change produces a real diff — a reviewer can see a five-minute bucket became one minute, and ask questions before it merges.
Branch, edit, commit — the change appears as a readable diff. Open a pull request, a teammate reviews it, and merging is what lesson 45's CI/CD pipeline actually reacts to.
Version control is the input CI/CD reacts to, with a human review step in front of it. Next up: infrastructure as code — ARM, Bicep, and Terraform basics.
